paragraphs: Having enough data to learn a pattern does not necessarily make that pattern computationally accessible. This paper studies that distinction in single- and multi-index models, which serve as settings for examining how learning methods discover features in high-dimensional data. Its central contribution is a quantity called the Noise Sensitivity Exponent, determined by the model’s activation function.

For single-index models with large additive noise, the authors show that this exponent fully characterizes when a computational bottleneck emerges. Within the broader regime they study, it also governs the existence and size of gaps between statistical possibility and computational difficulty. The result connects the activation’s sensitivity to noise with the difficulty of extracting learnable structure.

The authors then examine large separable multi-index models, focusing on the specialization transition where individual components become learnable. The same exponent controls a statistical-computational gap there. Together, these results offer a shared explanation for phenomena involving noise robustness, computational hardness, and feature specialization, within the model regimes covered by the analysis.
icml-2026-a-noise-sensitivity-exponent-c.tldr: An activation-dependent noise sensitivity exponent characterizes statistical-computational gaps across specified single- and multi-index learning regimes.

paragraphs: Adapting a pretrained generative flow to a reward and combining several flows are usually treated as separate problems. This paper places both inside one framework that operates on probability distributions. That formulation also supports doing both together: combining pretrained models while steering the resulting distribution toward a task-specific objective.

The framework expresses several ways to combine model densities. Intersections represent overlapping requirements, unions combine alternatives, and interpolation blends distributions. Reward-guided versions add a preference for desirable outputs. The authors also describe generative circuits that compose these operations into more complex logical expressions, giving model combination a richer vocabulary than a single blending rule.

To make the formulation usable, the paper introduces Reward-Guided Flow Merging, a mirror-descent procedure that turns the overall problem into successive standard fine-tuning tasks. The authors provide theoretical guarantees for both reward-guided merging and merging without rewards. They illustrate the method in visually interpretable settings and apply it to molecular design and low-energy conformer generation, demonstrating its use beyond simple examples.
icml-2026-a-unified-density-operator-vie.tldr: A probability-space framework unifies flow adaptation and model merging, with an algorithm that reduces reward-guided combination to repeated fine-tuning.

paragraphs: A sequential mean test examines incoming observations and decides when enough evidence has accumulated to stop. For bounded distributions, the test studied here already has a strong guarantee: as the allowed error level alpha approaches zero, its expected stopping time reaches an information-theoretic lower bound with the correct leading constants.

This paper asks a more detailed question about that stopping time: how does it fluctuate around its leading behavior? The authors first establish a central limit theorem for the KL-inf statistic underlying the test. This describes the statistic’s random deviations around its deterministic limit and supplies the foundation for analyzing the test’s timing.

They then prove that an appropriately centered stopping time, divided by the square root of log(1/alpha), converges in distribution to a Gaussian with an explicit variance. This second-order result describes variability that the leading expected-time guarantee leaves unresolved. Numerical experiments support the theory. The analysis remains within the stated setting of bounded distributions and a level-alpha, power-one sequential test.
icml-2026-beyond-first-order-asymptotics.tldr: A central limit theorem describes stopping-time fluctuations beyond the leading efficiency guarantee for a sequential mean test on bounded distributions.

paragraphs: Bayesian Forest Thompson Sampling uses Bayesian Additive Regression Trees to guide decisions in contextual bandit problems. It fits a separate reward model for each available action, allowing the expected reward to depend nonlinearly on context. Decisions use posterior draws generated through Markov chain Monte Carlo, so uncertainty in the reward estimates enters the action-selection process.

The paper also derives a Bayesian regret bound growing roughly as K times the square root of T, up to logarithmic factors, where K denotes the number of actions and T the decision horizon. This result is specifically for ideal posterior sampling under a correctly specified Bayesian design. Those conditions distinguish the theoretical guarantee from the practical procedure that uses MCMC draws.

Empirically, BFTS achieves competitive regret and near-nominal uncertainty calibration on nonlinear synthetic problems. It has the best average rank across nine OpenML bandit benchmarks and shows robustness to hyperparameter choices there. In a Drink Less trial case study, its estimated policy values exceed those of the compared linear, neural, and tree-ensemble methods.
icml-2026-bfts-thompson-sampling-with-ba.tldr: BFTS combines Bayesian regression trees with Thompson sampling, showing competitive empirical decisions and a conditional regret guarantee for ideal posterior sampling.

paragraphs: When a model makes a decision from both text and images, changes to the two inputs can interact. A robustness certificate covering only one input type does not cover that joint situation. This paper develops a randomized smoothing framework for inputs containing both discrete elements, such as tokens, and continuous elements, such as image values.

The method formulates the joint worst-case problem using Neyman–Pearson analysis. It studies how factorized discrete and continuous noise jointly order likelihoods, making the mixed-input calculation analytically manageable. The resulting certificate has a closed-form, one-dimensional representation and includes both Gaussian image smoothing and discrete text smoothing as special cases.

The authors validate the framework on multimodal safety filtering, where the relationship between text and image affects the decision. Their contribution is a model-agnostic certificate that addresses simultaneous token and image perturbations in this interaction-dependent setting. They describe it as the first such Neyman–Pearson certificate to their knowledge. Its significance is the ability to analyze heterogeneous changes together within one certification framework.
icml-2026-certified-robustness-under-het.tldr: A hybrid smoothing framework certifies robustness to joint discrete-text and continuous-image perturbations through a unified Neyman–Pearson analysis.

paragraphs: Evaluating an AI reviewer by its overlap with a human review can reward agreement without establishing correctness. Human reviews may overlook relevant issues or make mistakes themselves. CoCoReviewBench addresses this problem by changing how reference material is organized and checked, aiming to assess both the coverage and validity of an AI reviewer’s observations.

For completeness, the authors construct subsets for specific issue categories and omit an evaluation when the corresponding human review material is absent. This makes the available reference coverage part of the evaluation design. For correctness, they use discussions involving reviewers, authors, and meta-reviewers as expert annotations and filter reviews judged unreliable through that process.

The resulting benchmark contains 3,900 papers from ICLR and NeurIPS and supports more detailed evaluation of reviewing behavior. Its analysis finds that AI reviewers still struggle with correctness and produce hallucinated claims. Reasoning models perform more effectively as reviewers in the reported analysis. The benchmark therefore helps distinguish convincing review language from criticism supported by the paper and its expert discussion.
icml-2026-cocoreviewbench-a-completeness.tldr: CoCoReviewBench uses category-specific references and expert review discussions to assess AI reviewers’ completeness and correctness more reliably.

paragraphs: Understanding a complex fluid system requires modeling the range of states it can occupy. The paper targets learning these distributions from incomplete data consisting of multiple short trajectories across physical conditions. It also addresses difficulties posed by large, irregular geometries and regions where the fluid state changes sharply.

Condition-Aware Graph Flow Matching combines a flow that interpolates smoothly across physical conditions with a hierarchical graph representation. Its HieraGraphNet component models the graph-conditioned vector field through message passing at multiple graph levels. This lets the representation account for dynamics at different scales while exchanging information across distant parts of the system.

The authors additionally design graph coarsening around both connectivity and local geometric density, so the reduced graphs reflect the structure of the original geometry. They evaluate CGFM in three canonical scenarios spanning two- and three-dimensional dynamics and report better performance than state-of-the-art baselines. The approach brings condition dependence and geometric structure into the same distribution-learning method, directly addressing the two challenges motivating the work.
icml-2026-condition-aware-graph-flow-mat.tldr: CGFM combines condition-aware flow matching with hierarchical graphs to learn fluid-state distributions from incomplete trajectories across physical conditions.

paragraphs: An image’s relevance can depend on what happened elsewhere in a visual history. A system that compares a query with each image independently may miss that context. DeepImageSearch reframes retrieval as an exploration task in which an agent plans several steps and reasons over visual sequences to identify a target from implicit contextual clues.

The authors introduce DISBench to evaluate this capability using interconnected visual data. Creating suitable queries requires finding relationships across space and time, so their construction pipeline combines model assistance with human checking. Vision-language models discover candidate associations, reducing the context-discovery work that humans must perform before verifying the resulting material.

The paper also provides a modular agent baseline with fine-grained tools and a dual-memory system designed for extended navigation. Experiments find that DISBench remains challenging for state-of-the-art models. These results highlight a retrieval capability that isolated semantic matching does not adequately assess: following contextual relationships across a visual history to determine which image actually satisfies the request.
icml-2026-deepimagesearch-benchmarking-m.tldr: DeepImageSearch evaluates image retrieval that requires agents to explore visual histories and reason about context spanning multiple images.

paragraphs: Dynamic programming solves a sequence of decisions by working backward from later outcomes to earlier choices. When future values are estimated rather than known, each earlier calculation depends on approximations made downstream. This paper studies that dependency for discrete-time stochastic optimal control, placing the problem in a general framework suited to convergence analysis.

The proposed value-function estimator combines nonparametric regression with Monte Carlo subsampling. Kernel ridge regression operates within reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces, while Monte Carlo methods estimate continuation values. Together, these steps provide approximations to the quantities needed by the backward recursion, making their errors central to the reliability of the resulting value estimates.

The authors decompose the estimation error and rigorously control its components at each time step. They then analyze how those errors travel backward from the final stage to the initial decision. This connects local approximation accuracy to the behavior of the overall procedure. The paper illustrates the relevance of the analysis through American option pricing, showing how that application fits the same dynamic programming structure.
icml-2026-error-propagation-in-dynamic-p.tldr: The paper analyzes how regression and Monte Carlo estimation errors propagate backward through dynamic programming, with an application to American option pricing.

paragraphs: Audio deepfake detectors need testing data that exposes difficult synthetic speech, including examples underrepresented in existing benchmarks. FoeGlass automates this search using a language model’s in-context learning ability. It explores inputs to a text-to-speech system and looks for generated audio that fools a target detector, requiring only black-box access to the components.

The method builds its context using diversity measurements. This is intended to reduce mode collapse, where an automated search repeatedly discovers similar failures instead of covering a wider range of weaknesses. The resulting process generates challenging examples without manual supervision, addressing both the cost of collecting data and the difficulty of locating detector blind spots.

Experiments across several open-source speech generators and detectors report improvements of up to 94% in the false-negative-rate comparison used to assess the generated attack data. The discovered attacks also transfer across detectors. Separately, fine-tuning detectors on FoeGlass examples improves robustness by up to 41%, supporting their value for strengthening detection as well as evaluating it.
icml-2026-foeglass-simple-in-context-lea.tldr: FoeGlass uses black-box, diversity-guided language-model exploration to discover audio deepfake detector failures and generate data that improves detector robustness.

paragraphs: Removing several unwanted concepts from a text-to-image model can disrupt both forgetting effectiveness and ordinary image generation. Forget-It-All approaches this problem through model sparsity: it identifies concept-sensitive parts of the network and constructs masks that remove them. The framework performs this unlearning without training and requires little hyperparameter adjustment for new tasks.

Its first component, Contrastive Concept Saliency, estimates how much each weight connection contributes to a target concept. The method then combines temporal and spatial information to select neurons that respond consistently to that concept. It merges the resulting concept-specific masks into one mask for removing multiple targets together, while preserving neurons that broadly support general content generation.

Experiments covering three unlearning tasks report more reliable removal of multiple concepts alongside maintained image fidelity and quality. The stated contribution is a selective intervention that separates concept-specific responses from broadly useful generation behavior. This matters because the multi-concept setting requires coordinating several removals while keeping the model useful for content outside those targets.
icml-2026-forget-it-all-multi-concept-ma.tldr: Forget-It-All removes multiple image-generation concepts without training by merging masks of concept-sensitive neurons while preserving broadly useful neurons.

paragraphs: Some search requests cannot be answered correctly until the agent asks what the user means. InteractComp evaluates whether agents recognize that situation and seek clarification. Its questions are designed so that additional searching alone cannot identify the intended target: controlled ambiguity separates the target from plausible alternatives, and interaction supplies the missing information.

The benchmark contains 210 expert-curated questions across nine domains. Across 17 evaluated models, the best accuracy is 13.73%, compared with 71.50% when complete context is supplied. Requiring interaction produces large gains. The authors interpret this contrast as evidence of systematic overconfidence and failure to engage available interactive capability, rather than primarily a lack of reasoning ability.

A longitudinal analysis finds that interaction capability stagnated over 15 months even as search performance improved seven-fold. These findings expose a gap between retrieving information effectively and determining which information the user needs. The benchmark provides a way to evaluate that gap and, through the immediate feedback available in search tasks, a resource for training clarification behavior.
icml-2026-interactcomp-evaluating-search.tldr: InteractComp shows that search agents often fail to ask necessary clarifying questions, despite performing much better when given complete context.

paragraphs: Diffusion methods can produce visually strong image super-resolution results, but repeated sampling makes them expensive. One-step approaches reduce that cost, while introducing their own difficulties. This paper focuses on consistency models, identifying accumulated consistency drift and a failure called geometric decoupling, where pixel-level alignment does not preserve coherent image structure.

GTASR addresses these problems through a joint training approach. Its Trajectory Alignment strategy uses full-path projection to correct the tangent vector field describing the generative trajectory. Its Dual-Reference Structural Rectification mechanism adds explicit structural constraints. These components address complementary requirements: keeping the generation path consistent and keeping the reconstructed image’s geometry coherent.

The motivation is that fast inference needs more than agreement between pixel values along training paths. Structural relationships must also survive the reconstruction process. The authors report extensive experiments in which GTASR outperforms representative baselines while maintaining minimal latency. Their findings support this combination of trajectory and geometric constraints as an effective approach to one-step real-world image super-resolution.
icml-2026-joint-geometric-and-trajectory.tldr: GTASR combines trajectory alignment and structural constraints to improve one-step real-world image super-resolution while retaining low latency.

paragraphs: Concept Bottleneck Models make predictions through human-understandable concepts, giving users an interpretable intermediate representation. Their final task predictor, however, typically uses one expression with a functional form chosen in advance. This paper argues that the restriction limits both predictive accuracy and the ability to accommodate different users’ interpretability needs.

Mixture of Concept Bottleneck Experts expands that predictor along two dimensions: how many expressions it uses and what forms those expressions can take. The authors instantiate a linear version that learns a finite collection of linear expressions. They also introduce a symbolic version that discovers expert functions from data through symbolic regression, with users specifying which operators are available.

These choices make the mapping from concepts to predictions a more flexible part of the model design. A user can vary the number of experts and the permitted expression types to explore different balances between accuracy and interpretability. Empirical evaluation supports this framework for navigating that trade-off, rather than fixing the predictor’s structure before considering the task and user requirements.
icml-2026-mixture-of-concept-bottleneck-.tldr: Mixture of Concept Bottleneck Experts varies the number and form of concept-based prediction rules to explore the accuracy-interpretability trade-off.

paragraphs: Distributional reinforcement learning models the range of possible returns rather than only their expected value. Extending it to several return dimensions creates difficulties: familiar distribution comparisons may become expensive or fail to generalize naturally. Matrix-valued discounting adds another challenge because the corresponding Bellman updates need suitable contraction guarantees.

Sliced Distributional Reinforcement Learning compares multivariate return distributions through one-dimensional projections. This preserves access to tractable one-dimensional divergences. The authors prove Bellman contraction for uniform slicing when dimensions share a scalar discount, and introduce a maximum-slicing version with contraction under general dense discount matrices. These are distinct results tied to different slicing and discounting settings.

The framework supports several underlying divergences, with detailed analysis of Wasserstein, Cramér, and Maximum Mean Discrepancy choices. The paper also determines which variants fit the standard single-sample Bellman update, connecting mathematical properties to how distributional learning is implemented. Evaluations cover a toy chain, an image-based gridworld, and a subset of Atari games, examining the framework in several settings.
icml-2026-multivariate-distributional-re.tldr: SDRL uses one-dimensional projections to compare multivariate return distributions, with contraction results for different slicing and discounting settings.

paragraphs: Group Relative Policy Optimization is attractive for training tool-using language models because it converges quickly and does not require a value model. This paper investigates its training collapse in search-integrated question answering. The authors identify Lazy Likelihood Displacement: the probabilities of both correct and incorrect responses stagnate or decline early in training.

Their experiments describe a reinforcing failure process in which falling response likelihood produces low-confidence outputs, increasingly large gradients, and eventual collapse. Across the models studied, this follows three phases: initial stagnation, steady deterioration, and accelerated failure. The diagnosis connects an early change in response probabilities to the later instability of the optimization process.

The proposed LLDS regularizer activates only when a response action loses likelihood and targets only the responsible tokens. This selective intervention aims to preserve likelihood with minimal interference elsewhere. The authors report stable training, prevention of gradient explosion, and improvements across seven benchmarks, including relative gains of 45.2% for Qwen2.5-3B and 37.1% for Qwen2.5-7B over unmodified GRPO training.
icml-2026-on-group-relative-policy-optim.tldr: The paper traces search-agent GRPO collapse to declining response likelihood and introduces selective regularization that stabilizes the evaluated training runs.

paragraphs: A pretrained Transformer may learn from examples in its prompt yet struggle when those examples differ from its pretraining distribution. This paper studies attention temperature as an inference-time adjustment for that problem. Temperature controls attention selectivity, making it a direct way to change how the model uses the demonstrations it receives.

The theoretical analysis uses high-dimensional linear regression and an approximate-softmax attention mechanism that retains normalization and temperature-dependent selectivity. Within this setting, the authors derive a closed-form generalization error under distribution shift and an explicit temperature that minimizes it. The optimal value is linked to moments of the attention scores before normalization, giving an interpretable basis for adjustment.

The analysis also predicts conditions under which tuning temperature can recover near Bayes-optimal performance. Simulations support the theory, and experiments with pretrained language models show question-answering gains when noisy demonstrations induce distribution shift. Together, these findings support attention temperature as a lightweight robustness control, while the explicit optimality characterization belongs to the paper’s stated mathematical setting.
icml-2026-optimal-attention-temperature-.tldr: Attention-temperature tuning improves in-context learning under distribution shift, with an explicit optimum derived for a high-dimensional regression setting.

paragraphs: Clustering a directed graph is difficult because edge direction violates assumptions used by popular spectral methods. Those methods also carry the computational cost of eigen-decomposition. ParPIC approaches vertex clustering through random walks and power iteration, targeting weakly connected directed graphs and using diffusion behavior to represent their vertices.

The method builds embeddings from rows of an iterated diffusion operator. It introduces parametrized reversible random-walk operators, automatically selects how long diffusion should run, and truncates the final representation efficiently. These components address both the construction of useful graph representations and their computational cost. In particular, truncation produces lower-dimensional embeddings, reducing the complexity of the resulting representation.

Experiments on synthetic and real-world graphs find competitive clustering accuracy alongside improved scalability relative to spectral and teleportation-based approaches. The stated advantage is therefore a practical balance between clustering quality and computational demands. By combining a tunable walk, automatic diffusion timing, and compact embeddings, ParPIC adapts the power-iteration approach to the challenges of directed graph clustering.
icml-2026-parametrized-power-iteration-c.tldr: ParPIC clusters weakly connected directed graphs using tunable random walks, automatic diffusion timing, and compact embeddings for improved scalability.

paragraphs: Audio contains information about where sounds originate, but processing it as a mono stream leaves that spatial structure unused. Existing spatial audio systems face a different constraint: many depend on a fixed microphone layout. PhaseCoder addresses both issues with an encoder designed to work across microphone geometries and provide spatial information to a language model.

The transformer-only encoder receives raw multichannel audio together with microphone coordinates. It produces localization estimates and spatial embeddings, so its inputs explicitly describe the recording arrangement. The authors then fine-tune Gemma 3n to interpret the resulting Spatial Audio Tokens, connecting the encoder’s representation to language-model processing and reasoning.

PhaseCoder achieves state-of-the-art results on microphone-invariant localization benchmarks. The authors also demonstrate complex spatial reasoning and targeted transcription from arbitrary microphone arrays, describing this LLM capability as a first. The contribution connects flexible spatial sensing with language-based reasoning: the recording geometry is supplied as input, while the encoded spatial information becomes available for downstream audio understanding.
icml-2026-phasecoder-microphone-geometry.tldr: PhaseCoder encodes multichannel audio and microphone coordinates into spatial tokens that enable localization and spatial audio reasoning across microphone layouts.

paragraphs: SALSA-V generates synchronized audio from silent video, with an emphasis on long sequences and high sound quality. Its masked diffusion objective also permits audio-conditioned generation, so reference sound can participate in the synthesis process. The authors describe this design as supporting seamless audio sequences without a fixed length constraint.

A shortcut loss added during training reduces the number of sampling steps needed for generation. The model produces high-quality samples in as few as eight steps, without requiring separate fine-tuning or retraining for that capability. This moves the approach toward near-real-time applications while retaining the video-to-audio relationship that motivates the model.

Quantitative evaluation and a human listening study show significant improvements over existing state-of-the-art methods in audiovisual alignment and synchronization. Random masking during training additionally lets the model match the spectral characteristics of reference audio. That capability broadens the stated applications to Foley generation and sound design, where the sound’s character matters alongside its timing and correspondence with the visible action.
icml-2026-salsa-v-shortcut-augmented-lon.tldr: SALSA-V generates long, synchronized video-conditioned audio with reference-audio control and high-quality sampling in as few as eight steps.

paragraphs: An actor-critic trained on existing data can perform well initially yet lose performance as soon as online fine-tuning begins. The authors present evidence consistent with a landscape explanation: offline solutions and better online solutions may be separated by regions of poor performance that gradient-based updates pass through.

SMAC changes offline training to make the transition smoother. It regularizes the Q-function to satisfy a first-order derivative relationship between the policy’s score and the Q-function’s action gradient. The aim is to align the offline actor-critic with the optimization behavior it will encounter online, placing it where first-order updates can improve reward without first descending through a low-performing region.

Experimentally, SMAC finds offline solutions connected to better online solutions by optimization paths with monotonically increasing reward. It transfers smoothly to Soft Actor-Critic and TD3 across all six evaluated D4RL tasks. In four of the six environments, regret falls by 34–58% relative to the best baseline. These results support the proposed mechanism and transfer strategy in the tested settings.
icml-2026-smac-score-matched-actor-criti.tldr: SMAC aligns offline policy and value derivatives to enable smooth online fine-tuning, avoiding initial performance drops on all six evaluated D4RL tasks.

paragraphs: Tracking an object’s position and orientation can become unreliable when it is occluded or moves rapidly. Many existing pipelines also need CAD models, manual masks, or object-specific adaptation. STORM provides a unified reference-conditioned tracking framework that can start from one image with minimal manual input and includes a mechanism for recognizing tracking failure.

Its Hierarchical Spatial Fusion Attention combines reference and query information in a task-driven architecture. It supports either one reference or multiple references and can optionally use vision-language semantic information to resolve ambiguity between object instances. This gives the tracking system several ways to condition its predictions on the object it should follow.

A separately trained tracking verifier produces a continuous compatibility score that acts like an energy signal. STORM uses that signal to detect drift and automatically restart tracking. On LM-O and YCB-Video, experiments show improved annotation-free pose tracking over strong baselines, with reliable recovery from severe occlusion and rapid viewpoint changes at minimal overhead. Recovery is therefore an explicit part of the tracking framework.
icml-2026-storm-segment-track-and-object.tldr: STORM tracks object pose from a single reference image and uses a learned verifier to detect drift and trigger automatic recovery.

paragraphs: SWE-Bench Pro evaluates programming through complex software engineering work involving substantial repositories, enterprise applications, and changes across multiple files. Its central motivation is that success on traditional algorithmic problems leaves important professional development skills untested, including understanding existing systems and coordinating changes across a codebase.

The dataset contains 1,865 problems from 41 active repositories and spans 123 programming languages. It includes public problems from 11 repositories and private evaluation sets from 12 repositories across four problem categories. Keeping commercial evaluation material private serves evaluation integrity, while public examples provide access to representative engineering challenges. Tasks cover settings ranging from startups to enterprise applications.

The evaluation compares coding approaches and models under controlled conditions. Results vary substantially by problem category: traditional algorithmic challenges have higher success rates than complex engineering tasks involving multiple files. The reported gaps concentrate around contextual understanding, cross-file reasoning, and integration with large existing systems. The benchmark makes these dimensions of software work more visible in capability assessment.
icml-2026-swe-bench-pro-can-ai-agents-so.tldr: SWE-Bench Pro tests realistic repository-scale engineering and reveals substantial capability gaps on complex, multi-file tasks.

paragraphs: Software development continues across connected changes, so an agent’s earlier decisions can affect its ability to complete later work. SWE-Milestone evaluates that ongoing process. It focuses on preserving system integrity and limiting accumulated errors across streams of development goals, capabilities that isolated coding tasks do not directly measure.

To construct these streams, the authors introduce DeepCommit, an agentic pipeline that extracts verifiable milestone dependency graphs from noisy commit histories. A milestone groups work into a functionally cohesive goal. The resulting executable sequences preserve relationships among development steps, allowing evaluation to follow how an agent handles evolving requirements within the same software system.

Across 12 frontier models and four agent frameworks, reported performance falls from above 80% on isolated tasks to at most 38% in continuous settings. This large difference exposes difficulty with long-term maintenance and error propagation in the evaluated agents. The benchmark makes sustained development a distinct assessment target, showing why strong performance on individual tasks can coexist with much weaker performance across a connected sequence.
icml-2026-swe-milestone-evaluating-ai-ag.tldr: SWE-Milestone evaluates connected software-development sequences and finds a sharp performance drop when agents must maintain a system over time.

paragraphs: Observational studies can reveal causal relationships, but systematic bias can distort their conclusions. Existing approaches often detect that bias or attempt to reduce it. This paper asks a different diagnostic question: what process produced the bias, such as hidden confounding or the way participants were selected into the study?

The proposed method examines the relationship between bias magnitude and the predictive performance of nuisance-function estimators within the observational study. These estimators are auxiliary components of the causal analysis. The authors show that the way bias relates to their predictive performance can help distinguish common bias sources, turning that relationship into evidence about the mechanism behind an observed discrepancy.

Extensive synthetic experiments and a real-world case study support the method’s effectiveness at revealing bias mechanisms. The contribution adds a diagnostic perspective to causal inference: identifying that an estimate is biased and understanding why it is biased become separate analytical goals. The stated finding is that this relationship can help characterize common mechanisms, providing information relevant to improving observational causal analyses.
icml-2026-uncovering-bias-mechanisms-in-.tldr: Relationships between bias magnitude and nuisance-estimator predictive performance can help identify the mechanisms producing bias in observational studies.
